name: Ellagic acid
lead: Ellagic acid is a naturally occurring polyphenol, the dilactone of hexahydroxydiphenic acid, found in foods such as pomegranates, raspberries, strawberries, walnuts and grapes, where it is released from ellagitannins [11][12]. It is marketed as an antioxidant and, in some skin-care products, as a brightening ingredient.

Most research concerns its antioxidant activity and its gut-microbiota metabolites, the urolithins [1][3][6]. The sources reviewed contain no clinical trial of ellagic acid for skin brightening. Wikipedia reports that it is sold as a supplement with claims against cancer and other diseases, that there is no scientific evidence for such claims, and that the FDA has issued warning letters over such claims [12].
infobox: Low as free compound; metabolized by gut bacteria to urolithins

paras: Ellagic acid is formed by hydrolysis of ellagitannins and is described as poorly soluble in water [11][12]. Wikipedia lists chestnuts, walnuts, pecans, cranberries, raspberries, strawberries and grapes among foods containing it, with pomegranate juice a rich source [12]. Studies of pomegranate juice attribute much of its antioxidant activity to its phenolic composition, including punicalagin and ellagic acid [1][3].

Wikipedia reports that about 90% of ellagic acid is unabsorbed in the intestine until gut microflora metabolize it into urolithins, which are more bioavailable [12]. The biological significance of these metabolites, and the role of gut microbiota in polyphenol bioavailability, have been reviewed [6][7].

In vitro work reported antiproliferative, apoptotic and antioxidant activity of pomegranate polyphenols including ellagic acid, enhanced in combination with other polyphenols [3]. Reviews place polyphenols among dietary agents studied for cancer prevention, largely in preclinical settings [2][10]. Grokipedia notes that human clinical evidence for cancer and other conditions remains limited and preliminary [11].

No studies found on skin brightening or appearance use. Registered human trials involving ellagic acid or ellagitannin-rich foods address other outcomes: a trial in healthy men comparing ellagic acid from pomegranate juice with pure ellagic acid, a trial of a supplement for immune response to HPV infection, a phase 2 trial on metabolic syndrome components, and, in a further registered study, pharmacokinetics of pomegranate phenolics and urolithins [4][5][8]. A registered trial compared strawberry extract with hydrogen peroxide for tooth staining [9].

card.summary: A fruit-and-nut polyphenol sold as an antioxidant and brightener; no skin trials found.
card.note: Poor absorption; supplement health claims have drawn FDA warning letters.

quick.overview:
Ellagic acid is a polyphenol found in pomegranates, berries and walnuts, used in supplements and some skin-care products as an antioxidant or brightener.

Research is mostly laboratory-based; no trial of its brightening effect on skin was found.
quick.mechanism: It scavenges free radicals in laboratory assays and is converted by gut bacteria into urolithins, which are better absorbed than the parent compound.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports the FDA has warned supplement companies over disease claims. No safety profile was found in the sources reviewed.
